citations.quote: NASA Marshall Space Flight Center is currently working on a small satellite using an iodine fueled Hall thruster, called iSAT. This 12U satellite will be a technological demonstration of the use of a 200W Hall thruster in low earth orbit.

It is a 12 unit CubeSat with a size of 8" x 8" x 12", being used as a platform for a technological demonstration of an iodine Hall thruster propulsion system. $ ^{1} $ This will be done by starting at around a 600km circular orbit and reducing down to a 300km circular orbit with a 200W thruster.
SmallSats are typically constrained by volume, mass, and power, which limit their propulsive capability.

Integrating the system models into SysML with the requirements and system architecture allowed for an analysis of the power system. A simulation of the power system was completed providing insight into the design.

The preliminary power model for the iSAT is currently modeled in LabView and Excel, which produces an open loop set of values. By shifting over to a model based systems engineering approach, the power profile can be modeled throughout the orbit.
It also provides a platform that can leverage other powerful tools such as Satellite Toolkit and Matlab to simulate the satellite systems for a mission profile.
MBSE system models help keep all project activities (engineering, development, integration) consistent and track all the interfaces and dependencies in the system.
The integrated model simulates the mission to analyze the power requirements and the electrical power system for the iSAT. It transfers a previous analytical power model that used Excel into SysML.

This model is currently open loop providing basic outputs to inputs. This integration into a new environment allows the model to provide a closed loop orbit simulation with regards to the power system along with the supporting diagrams.

By showing that the power cycle is feasible for use, electric propulsion could expand its use on spacecraft. Furthermore using iodine as a propellant would provide a greater venue for electric propulsion on small satellites. This work would lower the uncertainty and risk associated with the use of electric propulsion.

The power model was previously completed by the Rotorcraft Systems Engineering and Simulation Center at the University of Alabama in Huntsville providing all the equations used in this analysis $ ^{13} $ . These equations are used to calculate the power generated from the solar panels, the power drawn from all the components and the energy provided to the batteries.

The solar flux, raw efficiency and the solar panel area are constants. The inherent degradation and MPPT efficiency are single input values. The temperature efficiency is a look up value and the eclipse factor and incidence angle are arrays.
Equation (2) multiplies the number of each component, N, by the current, I, and the voltage, V, of the component which are all single input values.

The available battery energy, $ E_{avalbatt} $ , is found by multiplying the energy generated by the solar cells, $ E_{sc} $ , by the maximum peak power tracking efficiency and subtracting the energy drawn.

These equations will only provide instantaneous values for the spacecraft. Using a software like Excel, time steps could be added to provide a temporal element but it does not provide a usable simulation. For this, the power model was transferred into SysML in Cameo Systems Modeler.

The SysML model of the iSAT started with defining the system architecture in a block definition diagram, defining the mechanical, propulsion, GNC, avionics, electrical power, and payload subsystems and electrical integration as blocks. These blocks are further defined into their composing components. For the subsystem blocks, the components are represented as parts and properties as values.
The model then moves to a requirement diagram. The 75 requirements are then traced through the mission success criteria leading to the system and component level requirements $ ^{14} $ .

With the components and requirements modeled, the focus can shift to the power system analysis through activity diagrams. The closed loop analysis is shown as an activity diagram which is broken down into the sun and eclipse calculations in figure 3.

To begin, a new package was defined for the analysis containing blocks, diagrams, and values pertaining to this simulation. The equations stated in the power models are represented as activity diagrams in this package.

To calculate the power generation, the activity diagram starts with a read self action which forks into read structural feature actions, referencing the values used in the equations, then which feeds into an opaque behavior providing the mathematical equation used. The output of this behavior is then fed to an add structural feature of P_gen, as shown in figure 4.

All parameters used in this activity diagram are found in the power tool block as parts under the power tool package. This is important because the read self action reads from the power tool package. Furthermore, the structural features are defined as the value types in the power tool block.

Instances were created for each component as the classifier with values for current, voltage and power mimicking the single input values. Then the subsystem's power draw can be calculated by summing up the components power.
Similar activity diagrams were built for each component.
The next step in the analysis is to calculate the battery level shown in figure 8. The battery level opaque behavior models equation 3 in SysML yielding the battery level.

Finally, the last step in the calculations is to increase the simulated elapsed time. Once the time reaches a certain value, the simulation transitions into the eclipse activities, which is the same as the sun battery level without the energy generation, completing the simulation as seen in figure 3.
Ultimately to run the simulation, a simulation configuration diagram was created.

block used an instance of the power tool populated with the parameters as the execution target. Furthermore, a Time Series Chart was set as the user interface to plot the charge level against the mission elapsed time. The results of each simulation are saved and placed into a results package which can be used for additional analysis.

While modeling the architecture and requirements was straight forward, simulating the power system was more nuanced. The first simulation completed was the stopwatch tutorial provided by NoMagic $ ^{15} $ . This introduced the use of read self, read structural feature, add structural feature, and opaque behaviors.

Moving forward a misunderstanding of the behavior of the read self action came clear. Since the component structural features were not under the same packages, the model was not able to read them. After consultation, the solution was found by associating the subsystems to the power tool block and increasing the read structural feature levels.
Once the execution logic was figured out, the values for the equations were inputted. With slight discrepancies in the voltage converter modeling, the values are similar to the previous power model.
The results of the simulation display a need for further refinement in the power model. Currently, there is no duty cycle which rapidly drains the battery, as shown in figure 9.

Also without an initial battery charge, the satellite does not produce enough power to last during the eclipse. However, all of these issues can be addressed by manipulating values within the model, such as providing an initial battery level or changing the efficiency levels once component level testing is done.
the SysML power simulation provides a powerful tool for the iSAT team at

Marshall Space Flight Center. In the same model, the power system can be analyzed beginning with orbit insertion and working through the mission profile. Moreover, if there is any change to the architecture it can be reflected in both the block definition diagram and the power system simulation.

Near future work for this power model is a 15 orbit simulation to analyze the charge state of the batteries for a propulsive maneuver. It is also the plan of the Complex Systems Integration Lab to combine the power model with propulsion and attitude control models to provide higher fidelity through the inclusion of STK and Matlab with other diagrams.

This paper shows that the iSAT electrical power system can be modeled in SysML. It not only provides a graphical representation of the system but also provides a means for simulation in the same environment.
This technology can be leveraged for a future mission to hopefully reduce the cost and unforeseen interactions.
